title: The seven books (the deuterocanon)
hook: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees are in Catholic Bibles; many Protestants call them the Apocrypha

segments.voice: Yesterday, three young men sang in the furnace and called every creature to praise. Your line was all ye works, bless the lord. What did you name? That song, by the way, is part of today's story. Day four hundred thirty-six.

Try this sometime. Put a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible side by side and count the books. The Catholic one has seventy-three. Most Protestant Bibles have sixty-six. The New Testaments match exactly, twenty-seven each. The difference is all in the Old Testament: forty-six books in one, thirty-nine in the other. Seven books, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel, like the song from the furnace we heard yesterday. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, and a different-sized shelf. So what are those seven, and how did that happen?
screen: `SEVENTY-THREE OR SIXTY-SIX.` → `THE NEW TESTAMENTS MATCH.` → `SEVEN BOOKS, AND SOME PASSAGES.`

segments.voice: The seven are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees. Catholics call them deuterocanonical. Canon comes from the Greek kanon, a straight rod used for measuring, and so a rule, and so the list of books measured as scripture. Deutero means second. The name dates from the sixteenth century, and the second doesn't mean second-rate. It means their place in the list was settled later, after some discussion. Catholics hold them to be inspired scripture, fully. Here's the history, as plainly as possible. Before Jesus, Jews in the Greek-speaking world used a Greek translation of their scriptures, the Septuagint, and its collections included these books. The early Church, mostly Greek-speaking, read that Bible. North African councils around the year 400 list them as scripture. Saint Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, had doubts and set them in a separate category, though he translated some of them anyway. In the 1500s Martin Luther gathered them into a separate section between the Testaments, calling them Apocrypha: books not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read. The Council of Trent in 1546 answered by defining the Catholic canon with all seven included. The King James Bible of 1611 printed them too, between the Testaments, though later editions often left them out. Today the Jewish Bible doesn't include them. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more. Most Protestant churches don't count them as scripture; Anglicans and Lutherans often read them for example of life. And in a Catholic Bible they sit right in among the others. Over the next week we'll open four of them.
screen: `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `SECOND, NOT SECOND-RATE.` · `SEPTUAGINT, JEROME, LUTHER, TRENT.` · `WHO READS THEM, AND HOW.` · then, large: `THE BOOKS BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Tobit in a Catholic Bible. If you have one nearby, open it to the table of contents now. In most Catholic Bibles, Tobit comes right after Nehemiah, followed by Judith. Find it, open to the first page, and read only the first verse. If you don't have one, picture the shelf instead: forty-six books, and seven you may never have opened. Settle, and breathe. Then ask yourself which part of the Bible you've never actually read. If you pray, you can ask for a little curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Deuterocanonical. The seven Old Testament books, and parts of Esther and Daniel, whose place in the canon was settled later; Catholics receive them as scripture. Today's word.
Your line: the books between. Today, read one page of Tobit, or just its first few verses, before tomorrow's lesson. Day four hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear readings from the deuterocanonical books at Mass, at weddings (Tobit), funerals (Wisdom) and in the prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees), the same as any other book of scripture.

original.note: Greek: a straight rod for measuring, a rule; the canon is the list of books measured as scripture.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholics added some books to the Bible.
what it means: seven books the early Church read in its Greek Bible, whose place was debated and then defined; churches still differ on them, and each can say why.
what a scholar hears: kanon, a measuring rod; deuterocanonical, a sixteenth-century term; Luther's 1534 Bible set them apart as Apocrypha, and Trent defined them in 1546.

sources.ref: Council of Trent, Session IV (8 April 1546), Decree on the Canonical Scriptures

notes: Book counts: Catholic 73 (46 OT + 27 NT), most Protestant 66 (39 + 27). Confirm.
'Deuterocanonical' is usually credited to Sixtus of Siena (Bibliotheca Sancta, 1566); the script says only 'the sixteenth century'. Confirm.
Luther's 1534 complete Bible placed these books between the Testaments with the heading describing them as not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read; paraphrased. Confirm.
Anglican Article VI: the Church reads them 'for example of life and instruction of manners'; paraphrased as 'for example of life'. Confirm wording is fair for Lutherans too, or limit to Anglicans.
Orthodox canons include additional books (e.g. 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Psalm 151, Prayer of Manasseh); 'a few more' used. Confirm.
Jerome's view: he distinguished these books in his prefaces but translated Tobit and Judith; confirm the summary.
Placement of Tobit after Nehemiah holds for most modern Catholic Bibles (NAB, RSV-CE, Jerusalem); in the Douay it follows 2 Esdras (Nehemias). Confirm.
